summary.label: SUMMARY
summary.heading: I ask a lot of questions before I write code.
body: I'm a full-stack engineer. I spent two years writing production code at Programiz Pro, a coding-education platform with over 100,000 paid learners. I built the course flow and learner dashboard, plus the engine that issues completion certificates. Most recently I led four engineers as technical lead during my internship at Jobss.ai, where I was responsible for authentication, role-based access, the employer workspace and the marketplace search.

During my Master's I built two connected systems from the data model up. One is a warehouse platform with lot-level inventory and state-machine fulfilment. The other is a multi-tenant Next.js storefront that shares stock with it. Day to day I work in React, Next.js, Node.js, TypeScript, PostgreSQL and Laravel.
Some of those questions sound obvious. I ask them anyway, because now and then the answer isn't what anyone assumed, and I'd rather find that out before the code exists.
I'm from Nepal and live in Melbourne, where I recently finished a Master's in Software Engineering. Outside work I read, travel when I can, and watch a lot of anime.

entries.product: Job and task distribution platform. Laravel and PHP, with Blade views built from Figma designs.
bullets: Technical lead for a team of four engineers. I made the architecture decisions and reviewed the team's code before it merged.
Built authentication and the role-based access control that separates employers from job seekers.
Designed the employer workspace. An employer posts a job or task there, then moves applicants through review, shortlist and rejection without leaving the page.
Marketplace search runs on a single index for both sides. Employers use it to find people, seekers use it to find work.
I picked cursor-based pagination over offset for the job and task feeds, because offset gets slower the deeper you page. Each feed is scoped to active dates.
Wrote the allocation logic that spreads available workers across open jobs and tasks based on demand.

entries.product: Coding-education platform behind programiz.com and programiz.pro, with over 100,000 paid learners.
bullets: Led Programiz Reports, a feature for beginners learning to program. Team of six, running Scrum. I gathered the requirements, decided the scope, ran sprint planning and took it from proposal to release.
Built the course flow and learner dashboard on programiz.pro, which paid learners use to work through and finish a course.
Built the certificate engine. Learners who finish a course get a verified completion certificate, and it has issued over 100,000 so far.
Wrote end-to-end tests in Playwright and Cypress and ran them in GitHub Actions CI.
Worked on the in-browser Python and JavaScript compilers on programiz.com. Visitors run code there without installing anything.
Integrated sensAI, the in-product tutor. Learners can ask it for help in the middle of an exercise.
Added Mixpanel and Microsoft Clarity to the landing pages, then rewrote the pages based on what people actually did on them.

entries.name: Nexus: warehouse management platform
entries.description: Personal project. I run an anime-apparel side business where stock kept going missing and I packed every order by hand, so during my Master's I built the system I wanted. Nexus syncs stock and order state with Aroma.
bullets: Modelled the warehouse as a labelled tree, so I can look up any item's exact location in seconds.
Product drops run through a state machine covering supplier onboarding, lot negotiation, intake and lot-level pricing. A drop can't jump a stage.
Stock movements go into a PostgreSQL ledger. I lock rows with SELECT FOR UPDATE, so two buyers can't claim the same unit.
Built lot-aware replenishment with a return-to-order path. A refund or exchange puts the stock back in the correct inventory state.
Wrote the fulfilment pipeline. It batches retail orders on a timer, and each order is its own state machine that I track until it completes.

codeNote.text: The repo is private because it runs a live side business. I can walk you through the data model and the state machines.

entries.name: Aroma: multi-tenant clothing e-commerce
entries.description: Personal project. A multi-tenant storefront where sellers run their own shop on shared infrastructure, with stock synced from Nexus.
bullets: Designed the tenancy model. Each seller gets an isolated storefront, and all of them run on one shared backend.
Built the buyer flow: search, product pages, cart, reservation, checkout and order history.

Catalogue pages use server rendering and static generation because they need to be indexed and load fast. Anything per-user is fetched on the client, with React Query holding the cache and Zustand holding the cart.
Ran Lighthouse on the product details page. Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) came in under two seconds.
Added an order-status view so buyers can track an order after paying. Sellers who only sell through social media can't offer that.

codeNote.text: The repo is private. It hasn't launched yet and it's wired into Nexus. Happy to walk through the tenancy model and how I split rendering.

earlier.name: Hospital E-Ticketing
earlier.summary: Hospitals and doctors register on the platform and open weekly appointment slots, and patients book online. The backend uses an inversion-test algorithm to stop double bookings across the Doctor, Patient and Hospital Admin roles.

earlier.name: Futsal Finder
earlier.summary: Tinder-style matchmaking for competitive futsal teams. Teams set their preferences and get paired with nearby opponents. It also had league and knockout tournaments, tiered battle seasons and court booking. This was the first full system I built.

aiEngineering.label: AI-ASSISTED ENGINEERING
aiEngineering.heading: How I use AI tools
body: I use agentic coding tools and give different jobs to different models. A light model explores the codebase, a stronger one drafts plans, and a mid-tier one writes the code.
I read and test every change before it merges, and I make the design calls. The tools save me time on boilerplate and on finding my way around code I haven't seen before.

I built Nexus and Aroma with spec-driven development. I wrote the spike, the reference implementation and the spec myself. Once the spec was frozen, I had the models plan and implement against it, and I reviewed what they produced.
